name: Angkor Wat
why: Published research used decorrelation stretch to clarify faint paintings of boats, animals, deities and buildings on the temple walls.
photo: Close, evenly lit color photographs of faded painted wall sections, including adjacent unpainted stone.
caveat: A carved relief and a surviving paint trace are different kinds of evidence. Match any interpretation to the original photograph.
sourceLabel: Tan et al., The hidden paintings of Angkor Wat, Antiquity (2014)

name: Göreme / Cappadocia
why: Surviving red motifs and figurative frescoes in rock-hewn churches offer color information on a painted surface. The included photograph focuses on worn red decoration.
photo: Close, evenly lit original photographs of worn painted sections, with some adjacent surface.
caveat: Surface damage alone does not identify who caused it or why. The photograph may include conservation work.
sourceLabel: UNESCO, Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia

name: Chehel Sotoun
why: The featured high-resolution photograph includes a painted narrative scene and worn ornamental borders. Try a border fit where pigment is patchy.
photo: Worn border details and original color documentation from before and after conservation.
caveat: The painting is historic, not prehistoric. Brilliant areas may offer little hidden detail. Do not infer intentional erasure or original hues from false colors.
sourceLabel: Amir Pashaei, original photograph and metadata

name: Bhimbetka
why: Surviving painted figures and faint neighboring traces make this a strong material match. A 17.9-megapixel photograph of Rock Shelter 8 is included.
photo: Close color views of the painted panel, preserving faint edges and some surrounding substrate.
caveat: Different paint layers, weathering and mineral staining can separate in similar ways. The app cannot date overlapping figures.
sourceLabel: UNESCO, Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka

name: Greek marble sphinx
why: The museum records surviving red, black and blue pigment on this original sphinx. The included open-access image supports an experiment on actual pigment traces.
photo: Close photographs of the wing, face and hair; fit to the sculpture rather than its studio backdrop.
caveat: Documented pigment is not a published test of this app. False colors do not reproduce the ancient palette. Avoid painted modern reconstructions as input.
sourceLabel: The Met, marble capital and finial in the form of a sphinx

name: Pompeii / House of the Vettii
why: The included Cyparissus image shows worn pigment and pale contours, providing a closer painted-surface example than a room overview.
photo: Straight-on high-resolution color photographs with the painting filling the frame.
caveat: Missing plaster cannot be recovered by color enhancement. Check conservation records before interpreting unusual boundaries.
sourceLabel: Original Cyparissus fresco photograph and metadata

name: Beni Hasan
why: A published DStretch study clarified obscure animal details in Egyptian tomb paintings, making this a direct precedent for photographic pigment enhancement.
photo: Tightly framed painted animals, outlines and faded details, with the wall evenly illuminated.
caveat: Compare with epigraphic records and conservation history before interpreting an unusual shape.
sourceLabel: Evans and Mourad, DStretch and Egyptian tomb paintings (2018)

name: Cueva San Borjitas
why: Jon Harman's algorithm description demonstrates enhanced pictographs here, including faint color differences in overlapping figures.
photo: Original color images of painted panels, with enough surrounding rock to compare pigment and substrate.
caveat: This app uses regularized RGB stretching; it does not reproduce DStretch's custom YDS or YBK presets.
sourceLabel: Jon Harman, DStretch algorithm description and examples

name: Tule River Painted Rock
why: The technique's author includes Tule River Painted Rock among his before-and-after rock-art demonstrations.
